extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry and drama (poets, playwrights, classicists)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for composing and evaluating poetic imitation (especially tragedy and epic), covering modes/objects/media of imitation, the parts of tragedy, unity, verisimilitude, plot devices (peripeteia/anagnorisis), character, diction, meter, and related standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (Imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (art) is imitation (mimesis) of actions; the poet imitates human action and life rather than merely reporting facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate actions that are or were or ought to be; choose what kind of actions to imitate (those that are noble, pitiable, fearful, exemplary). The imitation can be rendered through language, rhythm, and harmony; selection of what to imitate should serve the poetic end (pleasure/catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation (rhythm, language, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium by which imitation is effected is rhythm, language, and harmony (i.e., meter, diction, and music).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and combine the appropriate medium(s) for the genre: epic primarily uses language and meter; drama adds melody and spectacle. The medium influences how the imitation produces pleasure and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (what to imitate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet imitates human types, actions, characters and their moral qualities — not mere names or lists of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to imitate noble, significant actions and persons whose deeds and characters yield moral and emotional effects. The choice of objects affects verisimilitude and moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of imitation (narrative vs dramatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are different modes of imitation: e.g., epic (narrative) versus dramatic (acted) imitation; poets may narrate or enact actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to narrate (epic) or present through character and action (tragedy/comedy). Dramatic presentation tends to be more direct and concentrated; narrative allows length and multiplicity of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy — Plot (mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (mythos) is the first and most important part: the arrangement of incidents; it must be a complete whole with beginning, middle, end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots should be unified, causally coherent, of proper magnitude, and aim to produce pity and fear (leading to catharsis). Complex plots (including reversal and recognition) are superior to simple plots when well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy — Character (ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is the agent of the action: persons represented must be good (or of appropriate moral quality), consistent, and fitting to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be believable and appropriate to their roles; they need not be perfectly virtuous but should act in ways consistent with their nature. A character's mistake (hamartia) may bring about the tragic outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy — Thought (dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought denotes the faculty of saying what is proper to the circumstances — the themes, arguments, and reasoning presented through speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought should reflect the thinking appropriate to the character and situation and should contribute to the plot's demonstration of action and intention (the 'what' and 'why' behind deeds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy — Diction (lexis / elocution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words: the choice of phrasing, metaphor, and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elocution must be clear, fitting, and not merely ornate; avoid 'vacuitas rationis' (empty rhetoric) or language that obscures character or sense. Use meter and language suited to genre and scene (e.g., iambic for certain passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy — Melody (melos / song)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody is the musical element of the chorus and contributes to the pleasure of the imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate musical accompaniment and choral composition enhance tragic effect; melody is an integral but not the primary determinant of poetic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy — Spectacle (opsis / visual elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle comprises the visual components of dramatic presentation (scenery, stagecraft, gestures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle produces a powerful sensory effect but is least connected with the poet's art in terms of literary excellence; it supplements but does not replace plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must represent a whole: a complete action with a beginning, middle, and end (unity and completeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each incident should be necessary to the unity of the action; avoid disconnected episodes. The whole should achieve a natural and intelligible arc that culminates in the intended emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (proper length/size)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work must have an appropriate magnitude: not too long nor too short, sufficient to achieve its ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length should be judged by whether the action is completed and the effects are achieved without tediousness; epic can be longer because of its mode, whereas tragedy aims for a concise concentrated unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude and Necessity (probability or necessity of events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the poem should be either necessary or probable (verisimilar); the poet should not introduce happenings that lack rational grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fanciful or impossible inventions may be tolerated if they are plausible within the work or justified by 'what ought to be' (exemplar), and if the poet's skill disguises implausibility; but events that are gratuitously impossible or irrational are blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal) and Anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal and recognition are powerful plot devices: peripeteia (a sudden change of fortune) and anagnorisis (discovery/recognition) often combined to produce pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that successfully integrate reversal and recognition are superior; these devices should arise from probability or necessity, not arbitrary contrivance (examples discussed include Sophocles' Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia / Types of poetic error
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic errors are of two sorts: errors intrinsic to the poet's imitation itself (per se) and accidental errors (per accidens); hamartia (a slip or mistake) may bring misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge errors by whether they undermine the imitation's rationality; an error intrinsic to the depiction of something impossible is more blameworthy than an incidental fault. Distinguish culpable vice from honest mistake in characters and poetic invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate invention (what 'ought to be')
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may invent what 'ought to be' (qualia esse oportet) rather than strictly what is factual, provided it better serves the imitation and the ends of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invented particulars should correspond to what would most advantageously serve the art (improving on reality where necessary) and be credible within the poetic context; this is different from inventing the impossible without grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of irrelevant or vacuous material
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include speeches, episodes, or details that are empty of rational necessity (vacuitas rationis) or irrelevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate material that does not advance the plot, character development, or thematic demonstration; empty ornamentation that obscures morals or sense is blameworthy (anti-pattern: excessive rhetorical display that hides poor substance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of genre and form (epic vs tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the genre according to the kind of imitation desired: epic (long, narrative, many actions) versus tragedy (dramatic, concentrated, enacted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy is often superior in producing unified pleasure because of its concentrated imitation, music, and spectacle; epic allows breadth and multiplicity but risks dilution. Consider audience, means (chorus, music), and intended emotional effect when choosing form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate meter and diction for genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter and mode of speech should suit the genre and the part of the work (e.g., iambic or other meters where fit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meters and levels of diction appropriate to the characters and scenes; variation is permitted but must be suited to the imitation's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral propriety and the poet's responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Poet must consider the moral consequences of what is represented; improba (pernicious) portrayal without cause is censurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals that praise vice or obscure moral sense are to be avoided; when representing morally questionable acts, ensure they serve the imitation's didactic and emotional ends and do not promote impropriety gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion of parts (causal and formal connectedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: All parts of the poem must cohere: episodes, speeches, and scenes should be causally connected and proportionate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether each part contributes to the whole and whether the sequence of incidents follows from probability or necessity; disjointed multiplicity of actions undermines unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for refuting objections and errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When objections are raised against a poetic device or passage, solutions should be drawn from the forms of possible errors (e.g., impossible events, vacuity, impropriety, contradictory elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify objections according to their kind and answer via the prior taxonomy of what is allowable in imitation; e.g., show that an apparent impossibility was justified by probability or by the poet's invention of 'what ought to be.'
